prereg.desc: Bullish FVG formed at bar k: low[k] > high[k-2]; the middle bar k-1 is a bullish candle (close>open) that itself traded through the whole gap (low[k-1] <= high[k-2] and high[k-1] >= low[k], so session/weekend gaps are excluded); gap height low[k]-high[k-2] >= 0.5*ATR14 measured at the close of bar k-2 (before the displacement). Gap zone = [high[k-2], low[k]]. Track the gap from bar k+1 for at most 120 bars. The FIRST bar i>k whose low trades into the gap (low[i] <= low[k]) is the only retest considered: if that bar closes back above the gap top (close[i] > low[k]), i.e. it wicked into the imbalance and was rejected from it, go LONG at the open of bar i+1; if it closes inside or below the gap, the gap is mitigated and there is no trade. Stop anchor ext = min(low[k-2], low[k-1], low[i]) (the origin of the displacement and the retest wick), stop = ext - 0.25*ATR14(at close of i). Exit at the close of bar i+24 or at the stop; no take-profit. Bearish FVG is the exact mirror (high[k] < low[k-2], bearish middle bar spanning the gap, first retest high[i] >= high[k] with close[i] < high[k] -> SHORT, ext = max(high[k-2], high[k-1], high[i])). If several gaps get their first retest on the same bar in one direction, the most recently formed one defines ext; if long and short retests coincide on the same bar, no trade.
prereg.rationale: A three-bar imbalance marks a price range that traded only during one fast, one-directional bar: an aggressor (typically a large parent order or a forced/informed flow) lifted offers faster than liquidity replenished, so passive interest inside that range was never filled. Order flow is strongly autocorrelated (meta-orders are split over hours), so the same participant tends to keep working the remainder of the order passively at better prices; the first pullback into the unfilled range is where that resting/re-entering demand meets price. A retest bar that wicks into the gap and closes back outside it shows that this demand is still present and absorbed the pullback, so continuation in the displacement direction is expected over the following day. The stop sits beyond the origin of the displacement: if price returns there the imbalance is fully repaired and the order-flow story is falsified. Requiring the middle bar to span the gap ensures the imbalance came from trading, not from a session/weekend gap.
prereg.novelty: None of S1-S13, K1-K4, N1-N8 uses imbalances: they all fade (or follow failed) wicks through reference levels (PDH/PDL, PWH/PWL, Asian range, fractals, round numbers, clusters) or score sweeps with Kev. FVG1 needs no reference level at all; the event is defined by a three-bar displacement structure, the trade is WITH the displacement (a pullback continuation, not a reversal of an extension), the entry is on the first retest of the gap rather than on the bar that makes an extreme, and the stop is anchored at the displacement origin (wider than a wick stop).
prereg.notes: Direction (with displacement), retest = first touch only, rejection = close back outside the gap, stop beyond the formation origin are the textbook ICT definitions. Constants 0.5 ATR and 120 bars were fixed a priori as round values; only causality/event counts (eval_proposal.py check) were looked at before registration.

prereg.desc: r = log(close).diff(). Compression ratio at bar j: q[j] = std(r[j-11..j]) / std(r[j-119..j]) (rolling sample std, known at the close of bar j). Signal bar i requires q[i-1] < 0.4 (the market was compressed at the close of the previous bar). Box = [min(low[i-12..i-1]), max(high[i-12..i-1])] (the 12 compressed bars before i). The break must happen by trading, not by a gap: boxLow <= open[i] <= boxHigh. If close[i] > boxHigh -> LONG at the open of bar i+1 with stop anchor ext = boxLow (far side of the box); if close[i] < boxLow -> SHORT at the open of bar i+1 with ext = boxHigh. Stop = ext -/+ 0.25*ATR14 (ATR known at the close of bar i). Exit at the close of bar i+24 or at the stop; no take-profit; size 1. Later signals within 24 bars of a taken signal are ignored (harness thinning), so in practice this is the first close-breakout of a compression episode.
prereg.rationale: Realised volatility clusters and mean-reverts toward its recent norm, so a period whose 12-bar volatility is under 40% of its 120-bar volatility is followed by range expansion (confirmed non-directional effect, held out-of-sample including 2026). Compression is a low-participation equilibrium: dealers hold little inventory, liquidity is thin and both breakout-entry orders and protective stops cluster just beyond the obvious, tight box edges. When a bar CLOSES outside the box (acceptance, not a wick-and-reject), the stops and entry orders on that side have been triggered and the new information or session flow that broke the balance is being priced; with order flow autocorrelated over hours and the expected expansion still ahead, the expansion should be more likely to extend in the break direction than to travel back through the whole box. The stop beyond the far side of the box is the natural falsification point (a full traverse against the break means the box was a range, not a launch pad). Because the box height is several ATR, the round-trip cost is a small fraction of 1R, addressing the main failure mode of the sweep methods (stops ~0.8 ATR, costs 0.10-0.16R).
prereg.novelty: No reference level (PDH/PDL, PWH/PWL, Asian range, fractal, round number) and no sweep is involved. S5 faded sweeps that happened during compression; N6 followed the wick direction of a sweep (bar closed back INSIDE a level) 1-6 bars after a compression release. VREG1 requires the opposite bar type: a close OUTSIDE the compressed 12-bar box (acceptance), entered while the compression is still in force, traded in the break direction with the stop at the far side of the box (multi-ATR risk) instead of 0.25 ATR beyond a wick. It is a direction rule layered on the confirmed volatility-expansion effect rather than a level-reaction rule.
prereg.notes: data_informed=True only because the conditioning (12/120 std ratio < 0.4, 24h horizon) is taken from the confirmed NON-directional range-expansion result (b) supplied by the lead; no profit/loss, R or win rate of this rule or any variant was computed or seen. Constants were fixed before the first 'check'; only causality and event counts were inspected before registration. The gap filter (open[i] inside the box) mirrors FVG1's exclusion of session/weekend gaps so that the break is made by trading.

prereg.desc: Treat bar times as UTC and convert them to New York local time (America/New_York, DST-aware). Only Monday-Friday New York dates are used. For each New York date, the opening range (OR) is the high/low of the two H1 bars that open at 08:00 and 09:00 ET (i.e. 08:00-10:00 ET); both bars must exist, otherwise no trade that day. Then scan, in time order, the bars of the same date that open at 10:00, 11:00, ..., 15:00 ET (closing by 16:00 ET). The FIRST such bar whose close is above the OR high is a long signal; the FIRST whose close is below the OR low is a short signal; only the first close outside the OR counts (at most one signal per date, none if every bar closes inside). Enter at the open of the next bar. Stop anchor ext = the opposite side of the OR (OR low for longs, OR high for shorts), stop = ext -/+ 0.25*ATR14 (ATR14 of H1 bars, known at the close of the signal bar). No take-profit; time exit at the close of the 24th bar after entry (H=24). Same rule and clock on all four instruments.
prereg.rationale: All four instruments are USD-quoted, and 08:00-10:00 ET concentrates the main USD information events of the day: US scheduled macro releases at 08:30 ET (payrolls, CPI, retail sales, claims), the COMEX metals open (08:20 ET) and the US cash-equity open (09:30 ET), which since 2020 is also the most active period for crypto. Evans & Lyons (2008) show that a large share of the price effect of macro news reaches FX through order flow in the hours after the release, so price discovery is incomplete when the opening window ends; Gao, Han, Li & Zhou (2018, JFE) show the early part of the trading day predicts the rest of the day (late-informed and infrequent-rebalancing traders), with similar intraday momentum reported for crypto (Shen, Urquhart & Wang 2022) and commodity futures; the opening-range breakout is the classic implementation (Crabel 1990; Zarattini & Aziz 2023). A full H1 close outside the range after the window means post-window flow is confirming the opening reaction. The stop sits at the far side of the whole 2-hour range (typically 2-3 H1 ATR from entry), so the trade is wrong only if the entire opening reaction is reversed, and round-trip costs are a much smaller fraction of 1R than for 0.8-ATR sweep stops. Parameters are canonical, not tuned: the OR is the two clock hours containing 08:30 and 09:30 ET, the breakout window is the rest of the US cash session to 16:00 ET, pad 0.25 ATR and H=24 are the protocol defaults, ATR14 is standard.
prereg.novelty: None of S1-S13, K1-K4 or N1-N8 uses a clock-anchored session range or trades a full close beyond a level in the breakout direction: those methods fade or follow wick-sweeps (wick through, close back inside) of previous day/week extremes, the 00-07h Asian range, fractal swings or round numbers, with stops 0.25 ATR beyond the wick. SESS1's level is the same-day New York 08:00-10:00 ET range (DST-correct), the trigger is a close outside it, and the stop is the opposite side of that range. It is not an inversion of any failed method.

prereg.desc: Daily bars are built from H1 bars by trading day: the calendar date of the bar time, except that for USDJPY, XAUUSD and XAGUSD (markets closed on Saturday) bars stamped on a Sunday belong to the following Monday's day; SOLUSDT (24/7) uses plain calendar days. For each H1 bar i, U[i] = highest daily high and L[i] = lowest daily low of the 20 most recent COMPLETED trading days before the day of bar i (today's partial day excluded), and N[i] = mean daily true range (max(H-L, |H-Cprev|, |L-Cprev|)) of the same 20 completed days. LONG signal at bar i if close[i] > U[i] and close[i-1] <= U[i] (the first H1 close above the 20-day high); SHORT signal if close[i] < L[i] and close[i-1] >= L[i]. Enter at the open of bar i+1. Stop (ext, pad=0) = close[i] - side*2*N[i], i.e. two daily ATRs from the signal close (Turtle 2N stop). No take-profit. Exit at the close of bar i+240 (10 trading days of H1 bars for FX/metals, 10 calendar days for SOL) or at the stop. Size weight w = 1 (see notes: because R is measured in units of 2N, equal R weight IS inverse-volatility position sizing). Signals within 240 bars of a taken signal are ignored (harness thinning), so the system is flat-or-one-position, always in the direction of the most recent fresh 20-day breakout at entry time. Requires 20 completed trading days of history and N > 0.
prereg.rationale: Time-series momentum (Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen 2012; Hurst, Ooi & Pedersen's century-long study; the Turtle / Donchian channel rules used by CTAs since the 1960s-80s) is one of the best-replicated out-of-sample effects in FX and commodities. Proposed mechanisms: (1) slow diffusion of and under-reaction to fundamental information (central-bank policy divergence and carry for USDJPY, real rates / USD / industrial demand for gold and silver, flows into crypto), followed by delayed over-reaction as trend followers and momentum-chasing investors join; (2) hedging and risk-management flows that are pro-cyclical (option-gamma hedging when dealers are short gamma, stop-outs and margin calls of positioned traders, portfolio insurance), which push price further in the direction of a breakout; (3) a close beyond the prior 20-day extreme means the liquidity resting beyond the most visible multi-week level was consumed AND price was accepted there (the opposite of the failed sweeps faded in S1-S13): the participants whose stops sat there are now out, and the side that absorbed them was overwhelmed, which is informative about the imbalance that will keep working over the following days. The edge, if it exists, is small per day but persistent over weeks, so it must be harvested with a wide volatility stop (2 daily ATRs, about 10x the H1 ATR) and a long hold; that also makes round-trip costs a negligible fraction of 1R (USDJPY: 1 pip vs about 100+ pips of risk), which removes the failure mode of the sweep methods, whose 0.8-ATR H1 stops made costs 0.10-0.16R.
prereg.novelty: All 24 previous methods react to intraday liquidity levels (PDH/PDL, PWH/PWL, Asian range, 5-bar fractals, round numbers, clusters, equal highs/lows) with H1-ATR-sized stops and a 24-48 bar horizon, and nearly all FADE the wick (S11/N6 follow a failed sweep for 24 bars). TSMOM1 uses a multi-week reference (the 20-day Donchian channel built from completed daily bars), requires ACCEPTANCE (an H1 close beyond the channel, not a wick that closes back inside), always trades WITH the breakout, uses a daily-volatility stop (2N, about 10 H1 ATRs) and holds 240 bars. VREG1 (compression box breakout) also follows a close beyond a range, but its box is the last 12 H1 bars, it is conditioned on volatility compression, and it holds 24 bars with a box-width stop.
prereg.notes: data_informed=True is a conservative disclosure: the choice of the trend-following lens (follow an accepted breakout, wide stop, long hold) was suggested by the lead in the light of facts (a) and (c) (sweep fades have a gross edge smaller than costs because stops are tight; fading toward the opposite liquidity pool loses). The parameters themselves (20-day channel, 20-day N, 2N stop) are the canonical Turtle System 1 / Donchian values and were not chosen from any result; H=240 is the harness maximum (about the 10-day horizon of the Turtle System 1 exit). No profit/loss, R or win rate of this rule or any variant was computed or seen; only 'eval_proposal.py check' (causality and event counts) was run before registration. The Turtle 'skip a breakout if the previous one was a winner' filter is NOT used (it depends on trade outcomes). Weights: with risk = 2N, a position sized 1/N (Turtle unit, or MOP's 40%/sigma scaling) earns a dollar P&L proportional to R, so the equal-weight mean R already is the inverse-volatility-weighted result; an extra w = 1/vol would double-count. Bar times look like UTC (FX/metals weeks start with 1-3 Sunday bars at 21-23h), hence the Sunday->Monday fold so that no 1-3 bar 'day' enters the 20-day channel or N.

prereg.desc: Weeks = pandas periods 'W-SAT' of the bar timestamps (Sunday..Saturday). For every week W whose immediately preceding calendar week W-1 has >= 24 H1 bars and positive total volume: build W-1's volume profile with 24 equal-height price rows spanning [min low, max high] of W-1; each W-1 bar adds its volume to the rows in proportion to the overlap of the row with the bar's [low, high] (a zero-range bar puts all its volume in the row containing its price). POC = centre of the row with the largest volume (lowest row on an exact tie). In week W: if the first bar of W has low <= POC <= high (the week opened at value) there is no trade in W. Otherwise the approach side is fixed by that first bar: from ABOVE if its low > POC, from BELOW if its high < POC. The touch bar i is the first later bar of W that reaches the POC (low[i] <= POC when approaching from above; high[i] >= POC from below). Only this first touch is considered. If the touch bar closes back on the approach side (close[i] > POC from above -> LONG; close[i] < POC from below -> SHORT), enter at the open of bar i+1; if it closes at or through the POC there is no trade in W. Stop anchor ext = POC, stop = POC -/+ 1.0*ATR14 (ATR14 known at the close of bar i), i.e. one ATR beyond the level on the far side. No take-profit; exit at the close of the 24th bar after entry (H=24) or at the stop. At most one trade per week per instrument; size 1; same rule on all instruments.
prereg.rationale: The previous week's POC is the single price at which the most inventory changed hands last week, i.e. the modal cost basis of last week's positions. Once price has moved away from it, a large group of participants is holding positions opened there at a loss (those on the wrong side of the move) and another at a gain. The disposition effect and break-even anchoring (Shefrin & Statman 1985; Odean 1998; capital-gains-overhang and volume-weighted reference prices, Grinblatt & Han 2005) imply that the losing group is eager to exit flat when price first returns to its cost basis: shorts opened at the POC buy back there when price falls back to it from above, longs sell there when price rallies back to it from below, so the first return meets order flow opposing the approach. Auction-market (Market Profile) practice describes the same thing as the untested ('naked') POC acting as support/resistance on its first retest, because a high-volume node is where the other side previously showed up in size. The effect should be strongest on the FIRST touch (the break-even inventory is consumed by it) and only when price comes from away (a week that opens at value has no stranded inventory to release), hence those two filters; a close back on the approach side shows the opposing flow actually absorbed the touch. The stop is referenced to the level, not to the wick: if price trades a full ATR beyond the node the break-even supply/demand has been absorbed and the idea is falsified. With entry on the approach side and the stop one ATR beyond the level, 1R is typically 1-1.5 ATR, so round-trip costs are a smaller fraction of 1R than for the 0.8-ATR wick stops of the sweep methods.
prereg.novelty: No earlier method (S1-S13, K1-K4, N1-N8) or batch proposal (FVG1, SESS1, VREG1) uses volume at all. Their levels are price extremes (previous day/week high/low, Asian range, fractal swings, equal highs/lows, clusters of daily highs), round numbers or clock ranges; VOLN1's level is the mode of last week's traded-volume distribution, which normally lies INSIDE last week's range, away from the extremes where stops cluster, so the event is a return to an acceptance price, not a liquidity sweep beyond an extreme. Only the first touch per week is used, and only when the week opened away from the node (approach from away, at most one event per week). The stop is anchored to the level (1 ATR beyond the POC) rather than 0.25 ATR beyond the touch bar's wick, and there is no take-profit at an opposite liquidity pool (unlike N1). It is not an inversion of any failed method.
prereg.notes: data_informed=True only because the stop placement (anchored at the level with a 1-ATR pad instead of 0.25 ATR beyond a wick) was chosen knowing the lead's fact (a) that ~0.8-ATR stops make costs 0.10-0.16R; the level, the trade direction and every constant come from the cost-basis / Market-Profile argument above, not from any result. No profit/loss, R or win rate of this rule or any variant was computed or seen; only 'eval_proposal.py check' (causality + counts) was run before registration. Constants: 24 rows (volume-profile tool default), 1.0 ATR (one unit of hourly noise beyond the node), H=24 (protocol default), 24 bars minimum for the prior week (one trading day).

prereg.family: cross-asset relative value / residual (pairs) reversal, single leg
prereg.desc: Each instrument has one fixed partner: gold->silver, silver->gold, USDJPY->gold, SOLUSDT->silver. Partner alignment: for main bar i (open time t_i, closes at t_i+1h) the partner price Pc[i] is the close of the LAST partner bar whose open time is <= t_i, i.e. a partner bar that has closed at or before the close of bar i (as-of / backward merge on bar open times; partner bars after t_i are never used). Bar i is 'fresh' only if the partner has a bar with open time exactly t_i (partner market open at the signal hour). r[i] = log(close[i]/close[i-1]) of the main instrument, f[i] = log(Pc[i]/Pc[i-1]) (0 when the partner did not trade). At every bar j, over the W=480 main bars j-479..j: beta[j] = cov(r,f)/var(f) (OLS slope of r on f; the intercept/drift is not used) and residual vol s[j] = sqrt(var(r) - cov(r,f)^2/var(f)) (std of r - beta*f; sample moments). The estimation window is lagged by K=24 bars so it does not overlap the divergence window: b[i] = beta[i-24], sd[i] = s[i-24]. 24-bar residual: e[i] = log(close[i]/close[i-24]) - b[i]*log(Pc[i]/Pc[i-24]); z[i] = e[i] / (sd[i]*sqrt(24)). SHORT signal at bar i if z[i] >= 2 and z[i-1] < 2 (first bar whose 1-day move is 2 sigma richer than the partner implies); LONG signal if z[i] <= -2 and z[i-1] > -2. Bar i must be fresh and all quantities finite with var(f) > 0. Enter at the open of bar i+1. Stop (ext, pad=0) = close[i]*exp(-side*1.0*sd[i]*sqrt(24)), i.e. one further 24-bar residual sigma against the position measured from the signal close (the residual going from 2 to 3 sigma if the partner stays put). No take-profit. Exit at the close of bar i+24 or at the stop. Weight w = 1. atr = ATR14 of the main instrument at the close of bar i (used only by the harness's minimum-risk check). Signals within 24 bars of a taken signal are ignored (harness thinning).
prereg.rationale: Gold and silver share their main drivers (USD, US real yields, risk appetite; H1 return correlation about 0.74), and USDJPY and gold are linked through the same US real-yield/USD channel and opposite safe-haven roles (correlation about -0.35). A one-day move of one market that its linked market does NOT confirm is, on average, less likely to be news about the shared fundamental and more likely to be market-specific liquidity demand: a large parent order or ETF creation/redemption flow in one metal, option-hedging or stop cascades in one contract, positioning squeezes in one futures market. Liquidity providers and relative-value desks that trade the gold/silver ratio or gold-in-yen absorb that flow only at a price concession, which is repaid as the deviation decays (Grossman & Miller 1988 liquidity provision; Gatev, Goetzmann & Rouwenhorst 2006 pairs trading with a 2-sigma open rule; Avellaneda & Lee 2010 residual s-scores; Da, Liu & Schaumburg 2014 show the short-term reversal sits in the residual, not the factor component). The part of the move explained by the partner is treated as information and is NOT faded, because the residual removes it via the rolling hedge ratio. Trading one leg keeps the common-factor exposure unhedged; that adds noise but no expected loss. The stop is set in units of the residual's own daily volatility (median about 1.8-2.5 H1 ATR14, versus about 0.8 ATR for the sweep stops), so the round-trip cost is a smaller fraction of 1R, avoiding the failure mode of the sweep methods (0.8-ATR stops, costs 0.10-0.16R).
prereg.novelty: Only N2 (gold/silver SMT divergence) of the 24 prior methods used a second instrument, and it was a liquidity-level event: one metal swept its previous-day high/low while the other did not, faded with a stop 0.25 ATR beyond the wick. XAS1 uses no level, sweep or wick at all: the event is a statistical one, a 2-sigma 24-bar residual from a rolling 20-day hedge regression on a linked market, applied to all four instruments (USDJPY hedged with gold, SOL with silver), with a residual-volatility stop (median 1.8-2.5 ATR14 from the signal close) and a 24-bar time exit. It is not an inversion of any failed method (it trades the same convergence direction as N2, chosen from the pairs-trading prior, not from N2's result).
prereg.notes: Constants are canonical, not tuned: K=24 (one day), W=480 (about 20 trading days, the standard 1-month window), 2-sigma entry (Gatev et al.), stop at a further 1 sigma (pairs 'spread at 3 sigma' stop), H=24 = K. Before writing the rule I looked only at INPUT properties of pre-2026 data, never at any forward return, R, P/L or win rate: (1) cross-correlations of H1 log returns at lags -3..+3 peak at lag 0 for every pair and are ~0 at +-1 (e.g. gold/silver 0.739 at lag 0, |r|<0.02 at +-1; USDJPY/gold -0.351 vs |r|<0.015), so the four series share one clock and the same open-time labelling; a partner bar with the same open time as the main bar closes at the same instant as the main bar, so using it at the signal close is causal. (2) SOL's correlation with silver/gold/USDJPY is 0.11/0.08/-0.02; silver was the a-priori choice (pro-cyclical metal) and is also the largest. Consequence: for SOL the hedge removes only ~1% of variance, so the SOL leg is close to a plain 24-bar own-move fade; USDJPY removes ~12%; the metals ~55%. CAUSALITY of the cross-asset input: the harness's corruption test only perturbs the main instrument, so the partner path is guarded by construction: partner bars are taken by searchsorted(partner open times, t_i, side='right')-1 (no partner bar with open time > t_i can be selected), all rolling windows are trailing, shifts are positive, and the partner file is loaded with include_holdout only when the main df itself extends into 2026 (pre-2026 rows are identical either way). STRUCTURAL LIMIT (please read): every partner series starts in 2018-03 (metals) or 2020-08 (SOL), so the USDJPY leg can only fire from about 2018-04 onward; the USDJPY 2011-2015 era has 0 events and P2 cannot be met by any cross-asset rule on this data. The USDJPY 2016-2020 era contains only 2018-2020 events. Extra causality test run by the designer (input-only, no outcomes): for 10 random signals per instrument, partner bars with open time > t were replaced by noise, and separately the partner series was truncated at t; signals at t were unchanged in 80/80 cases; truncating the main series mid-sample left all earlier signals identical. Check counts (non-overlapping, pre-2026): USDJPY 308 (2018-2025), SOL 233, gold 293, silver 269. Stop distance |close-ext|/ATR14 median: USDJPY 2.40, SOL 2.45, gold 1.86, silver 1.75; median rolling beta: USDJPY on gold -0.22, SOL on silver 0.34, gold on silver 0.39, silver on gold 1.51.

prereg.family: calendar flow: month-end London-fix price-pressure reversal
prereg.desc: Map bar open times (UTC) to London local time (Europe/London, DST-aware). Month-end day = the last Monday-Friday date of each calendar month by the London calendar (calendar rule only, holidays ignored: a London date d with weekday Mon-Fri is month-end if the next weekday after d falls in a different month). On each month-end day take the H1 bar that opens at 08:00 London (session open price O = its open) and the H1 bar that opens at 15:00 London (signal bar, it closes at 16:00 London = the WM/Refinitiv 4pm fix; its close C). Both bars must exist on that London date, otherwise no trade that month. Session move m = C - O. If m > 0 go SHORT, if m < 0 go LONG (fade the London-session move into the month-end fix); m == 0: no trade. At most one signal per month. Enter at the open of the next bar (16:00 London). Stop: ext = C - side*2.0*ATR14 with pad = 0, i.e. a fixed volatility stop 2.0 x ATR14 (H1 ATR14 including the signal bar, known at its close) from the signal close. No take-profit; time exit at the close of the 24th bar after entry (H=24). Same rule, clock and parameters on all four instruments; no filters, no weights.
prereg.rationale: Month-end is the most predictable liquidity-demand window in USD markets: global portfolio managers rebalance currency hedges and multi-asset weights, and pay/collect cash, at the month-end London 4pm WM/Refinitiv fix, so large uninformed orders arrive at a known time. Dealers that take fix orders pre-position during the London session, pushing prices in the direction of the net flow; once the fix prints the demand is gone and the inventory-driven price pressure should partly revert (temporary price impact compensating liquidity providers: Grossman & Miller 1988; Campbell, Grossman & Wang 1993). This pattern is reported for FX around the London fix and is strongest at month-end (Melvin & Prins 2015, month-end equity-hedge rebalancing at the 4pm fix; Evans 2018, price behaviour around the WMR fix; Krohn, Mueller & Whelan 2024, dollar moves into fixes that reverse afterwards), and month-turn institutional cash needs move USD and asset prices (Etula, Rinne, Suominen & Vaittinen 2020, 'Dash for Cash'); the same pre-fix / post-fix reversal is documented at the Tokyo fix (Ito & Yamada 2017). Because the sign of the month-end flow changes month to month (it depends on that month's relative asset performance, which we do not observe), the rule infers it from the price itself: the London-session move into the fix is taken as the footprint of the flow and faded after the fix. All four instruments are USD-quoted, so USD-side month-end demand reaches each of them; the metals also have their LBMA benchmark auctions inside the window (silver 12:00, gold 15:00 London), which is where month-end fund rebalancing in metals executes; crypto reference rates used for fund valuation and futures settlement (CME CF, computed 15:00-16:00 London) put the crypto month-end flow in the same hour. The SOL link is the weakest part of the story and is stated as such. Parameters are canonical, not tuned: last business day of the month, London session open (08:00) to the 4pm fix, H=24 (protocol default: the first trading day of the new month), and a standard 2 x ATR volatility stop. The stop width was set wide on purpose so that round-trip costs are a small fraction of 1R (~0.03-0.05R on all four instruments), in light of the REPORT's cost diagnostic for 0.8-ATR sweep stops; it was not chosen from any result of this rule.
prereg.novelty: None of the 24 tested methods (S1-S13, K1-K3, N1-N8) uses the calendar: they are all price-level wick-sweep fades/follows (previous day/week extremes, Asian range, fractal swings, round numbers, equal highs/lows, multi-day clusters) or Kev judgements of such sweeps; N8 used a clock window (Monday 00-06h) but still traded a sweep of the previous week's high/low. CAL1 has no level and no sweep: it trades once a month at a scheduled flow event (the month-end 4pm London fix), its direction comes from the session move into that event, and its stop is a 2-ATR volatility stop rather than 0.25 ATR beyond a wick. It is not an inversion of any failed method, and it differs from the batch's SESS1 (daily New York opening-range breakout, follow) in calendar, session, trigger and direction.

prereg.family: stop cascade through a fresh major level (follow)
prereg.desc: ATR = sweep_lib.atr(df) (14-bar mean true range). Levels from sweep_lib.levels(df, name): PDH/PDL (previous completed calendar day's high/low on the bar clock), PWH/PWL (previous completed calendar week's high/low, pandas period 'W'), RNU/RND (round number just above/below the bar's own open: USDJPY whole yen, SOL multiples of 5, gold multiples of 25, silver multiples of 0.5). Signal bar i, LONG cascade: (a) range shock: high[i]-low[i] >= 3.0*ATR[i-1] (ATR known at the close of the previous bar); (b) for at least one upper level X in {PDH, PWH, RNU}: open[i] < X < close[i] (opened below the level, closed above it, so the level was crossed by trading inside bar i) AND the level was still intact before bar i: the highest high of the bars of the same calendar day before bar i is < X for PDH and RNU, and the highest high of the bars of the same calendar week before bar i is < X for PWH (no earlier bar of the period -> intact); (c) close in the outer half of the bar: close[i]-low[i] >= 0.5*(high[i]-low[i]). SHORT cascade is the mirror image with lower levels {PDL, PWL, RND}: high-low >= 3*ATR[i-1], open[i] > X > close[i], the lowest low of the same day (week for PWL) before bar i is > X, and high[i]-close[i] >= 0.5*(high[i]-low[i]). Several levels crossed by one bar give one signal. Trade: FOLLOW the cascade (LONG after a long cascade, SHORT after a short one) at the open of bar i+1; stop anchor ext = the cascade bar's opposite extreme (low[i] for longs, high[i] for shorts), stop = ext -/+ 0.25*ATR[i] (ATR known at the close of bar i); no take-profit; exit at the close of the 24th bar after entry (H=24) or at the stop. Size 1; same rule on all four instruments; overlapping signals are thinned by the harness (gap 24 bars).
prereg.rationale: Resting stop-loss orders cluster just beyond the most visible reference prices: yesterday's and last week's extremes and round numbers (Osler 2003, 2005, using actual stop-loss order books of a major FX dealer: stop-loss buy orders sit just above round numbers and recent highs, take-profit orders AT them). When a stop-loss cluster is triggered, the stops become market orders in the direction of the move; dealers who fill them re-hedge in the same direction, which can trigger the next cluster, so stop-loss orders produce 'price cascades' -- trends that are faster and more persistent after a level is crossed (Osler 2005, JIMF). Two conditions separate a true cascade from a sweep (the sweep fades studied in S1-S13, N4): the bar must CLOSE beyond the level and in the outer half of its range, i.e. the flow released by the stops was absorbed and price was accepted beyond the level instead of being rejected; and the bar must be a range shock (>= 3x ATR), i.e. the order flow was large relative to normal liquidity -- the size at which an imbalance is too big to be absorbed by the passive side within the hour. The 'fresh level' filter keeps only first crossings in the period, where the stop cluster is still intact (a level already traded through earlier that day has had its stops consumed). Why the move should continue past the next open: (i) the inventory of the dealers who absorbed the cascade is left on the losing side and is worked off over the following hours, (ii) a range shock often carries information (news, intervention, liquidation) to which slower participants (real-money, risk-parity, option delta hedgers short gamma) adjust gradually, (iii) the forced sellers/buyers are not finished: positions whose stops sit further away are now closer to them. Range shocks are known (fact (b), held out-of-sample) to be followed by a larger next-24h range, so the 24-bar exit sits in the window where the price will move the most; this proposal tests whether, when the shock is a fresh-level cascade with acceptance, that move is directional. Structurally the stop is the cascade bar's far extreme, at least ~1.5 ATR from entry, so the round-trip cost is a small fraction of 1R (fact (a): the 0.8-ATR wick stops made costs 0.10-0.16R).
prereg.novelty: No earlier method follows a single-bar stop cascade. S1-S13, N1, N4, N5, N8 all FADE bars that wick through a level and close back inside (the opposite close condition). S11 follows a FAILED SWEEP: it needs a prior sweep bar that closed back inside, then a later close beyond the sweep's extreme within 3 bars, has no size condition and no fresh-level condition; EXH1 needs no sweep, the level is crossed and closed beyond by one bar that is itself a >= 3x ATR range shock closing in its outer half. N4 fades a second sweep within 24 bars of a first one; EXH1 requires that the level was NOT traded through earlier in the day/week, and trades in the direction of the break. N6 follows a sweep near a compression release (vol-ratio trigger, sweep bar closes back inside); EXH1 has no compression condition and uses the range-shock trigger of fact (b). TSMOM1 (batch) follows the first H1 close beyond a 20-day Donchian channel with no bar-size condition and a 2N/10-day exit; VREG1 follows a close out of a 12-bar compression box; SESS1 is a New-York opening-range breakout. EXH1's levels are one-day/one-week extremes and round numbers, the trigger is the size of the crossing bar, the stop is the cascade bar's opposite extreme, and the exit is 24 bars.
prereg.notes: data_informed=True because (1) the range-shock threshold (3x prior ATR) is taken from the lead's fact (b), an empirical non-directional result, and (2) the wide stop (cascade bar's far extreme) was chosen knowing fact (a) that 0.8-ATR stops make costs 0.10-0.16R. The trade direction (follow) comes from Osler's stop-loss cascade evidence, not from inverting any failed method's result. No profit/loss, R or win rate of this rule or any variant was computed or seen; only 'eval_proposal.py check' (causality + counts) was run before registration.

prereg.family: liquidity magnet: approach to an untaken prior-day/prior-week extreme (tp at the pool)
prereg.desc: Trading day: for USDJPY, XAUUSD, XAGUSD the FX convention, the day rolls at 17:00 New York time (bar open times are treated as UTC, converted to America/New_York DST-aware, shifted +7h, date taken; so Sunday-evening bars belong to Monday); for SOLUSDT the UTC calendar date. Trading week = pandas period 'W' (Mon..Sun) of the trading day. PDH/PDL = high/low of the previous trading day present in the data; PWH/PWL = high/low of the previous trading week present in the data (both fully completed before the current day/week starts). At the close of bar i: PDH is UNTAKEN if every bar of the current trading day up to and including bar i has high < PDH; PDL untaken if every such bar has low > PDL; PWH (PWL) untaken if every bar of the current trading week up to and including i has high < PWH (low > PWL). U[i] = the nearest untaken upper pool = min of the untaken values among {PDH, PWH} (none -> no upper magnet); D[i] = the nearest untaken lower pool = max of the untaken values among {PDL, PWL}. A = ATR14 = sweep_lib.atr(df) at the close of bar i. Upper zone flag zu[i] = U exists and U[i] - close[i] <= 1.0*A[i]; lower zone flag zd[i] = D exists and close[i] - D[i] <= 1.0*A[i]. LONG signal at bar i if zu[i] and not zu[i-1] (the close has just come within one ATR of an untaken upper pool, or a new untaken pool has just appeared within one ATR) and not zd[i]; SHORT signal if zd[i] and not zd[i-1] and not zu[i]. If price is within one ATR of untaken pools on both sides there is no trade. Enter at the open of bar i+1. Take-profit tp = U[i] for longs, D[i] for shorts (exactly at the pool). Stop: ext = close[i] - side*1.0*A[i], pad = 0, i.e. one ATR beyond the signal close on the side away from the magnet. Exit at tp, at the stop, or at the close of the 24th bar after entry (H=24). Size 1. Same rule on all four instruments; overlapping signals are thinned by the harness (gap 24 bars).
prereg.rationale: Prior-day and prior-week highs/lows are where stop-loss orders of positioned traders and breakout entry stops cluster (Osler 2003, 2005: stop-loss orders in FX cluster just beyond salient prior extremes and round numbers, and their execution produces fast, self-reinforcing price cascades). Such an untaken pool is a source of liquidity: a large participant who needs to buy (sell) size fills best against the burst of sell (buy) orders the triggered stops release, and dealers who see the clustered orders in their books, as well as short-horizon traders who anticipate the cascade, profit from pushing price the final stretch into the pool. That incentive exists only while the pool is still untaken (its orders have not been consumed) and is strongest when it is close, i.e. within one typical hourly range. So the hypothesis is that once price is within one ATR of an untaken pool, the probability of touching the pool before moving one ATR the other way is higher than the martingale value implied by the distances. The trade harvests only this run-in leg and exits AT the pool, before the partial reversal that the sweep-fade literature (fact a: small gross reversal after a sweep) documents on the other side of the level; both facts are consistent with the same stop-hunt cycle (attraction -> run -> exhaustion).
prereg.novelty: None of the 24 methods in REPORT.md (S1-S13, K1-K3, N1-N8) nor the registered batch proposals trades the APPROACH to a level: S1-S13, N4, N5, N8 fade a wick through a level after it was swept; S11 and EXH1 follow after the level has broken; N1 fades a sweep toward the OPPOSITE pool. MAG1 differs from N1 on every axis: (1) there is no sweep or reversal trigger, the event is price entering a one-ATR zone below (above) an untaken pool, so the trade is usually WITH the recent move rather than against an extreme; (2) the target is the NEAREST untaken pool and must be within 1 ATR, whereas N1 required the opposite pool to be at least 2 ATR away (low hit rate); (3) the stop is a fixed one ATR from the signal close (symmetric to the zone) instead of a ~0.8 ATR wick stop, and the exit is at the pool before any sweep happens. It also differs from VOLN1 (fades a first touch of a volume node, no tp) and TSMOM1 (20-day breakout follow).
prereg.notes: data_informed=True: choosing a NEAR target and an approach (non-reversal) entry was shaped by knowing that N1 (sweep fade toward a far opposite pool) lost about 0.2R everywhere and that sweep fades have only a small gross edge. No P/L of this rule or any variant was computed; only eval_proposal.py check (causality + counts) was run before registration. Day roll at 17:00 New York is the standard FX/metals trading-day convention (bar times look like UTC: FX Sunday bars at 21-23h, metals at 22-23h, last Friday bar 21h); SOL uses the standard UTC daily candle.

prereg.family: multi-timeframe: daily-trend pullback, H1 sweep-and-reclaim of the prior-day extreme
prereg.desc: Trading day of each H1 bar: USDJPY/XAUUSD/XAGUSD: convert the bar open time from UTC to America/New_York (DST-aware), add 7 hours, take the date (day runs 17:00-17:00 New York; Sunday-evening bars belong to Monday). SOLUSDT: UTC calendar date. Daily bar of a trading day = open of its first H1 bar, max high, min low, close of its last H1 bar; only days with >= 12 H1 bars are valid daily bars. For an H1 bar i in trading day d, 'prior day' P = the most recent VALID trading day strictly before d (always fully closed before bar i opens). From the valid daily series up to and including P: PDH = high[P], PDL = low[P]; SMA20 = mean of the 20 valid daily closes ending at P; ATRd = mean over the 14 valid days ending at P of the daily true range max(H-L, |H-Cprev|, |L-Cprev|) (Cprev = previous valid daily close). Daily uptrend if close[P] > SMA20, downtrend if close[P] < SMA20 (needs 20 and 15 valid days of history). LONG signal at H1 bar i: daily uptrend AND open[i] > PDL AND low[i] < PDL AND close[i] > PDL (the bar wicked through the prior-day low and closed back above it) AND no earlier H1 bar of the same trading day d traded below PDL (min low of bars of day d before i >= PDL; the first bar of the day passes), i.e. only the first breach of the prior-day low in the day. SHORT signal: mirror image in a daily downtrend with PDH (open[i] < PDH, high[i] > PDH, close[i] < PDH, max high of earlier bars of day d <= PDH). Only the trend side is ever traded (PDL sweeps in uptrends, PDH sweeps in downtrends), so there is at most one signal per trading day. Enter at the open of bar i+1. Stop anchor ext = the sweep wick (low[i] for longs, high[i] for shorts); atr column = ATRd (daily ATR known at the close of bar i); pad = 0.25, so stop = wick -/+ 0.25 x daily ATR14. No take-profit; exit at the close of the 24th bar after entry (H=24) or at the stop. Size 1. Same rule, clock and constants on all four instruments; signals within 24 bars of a taken signal are dropped by harness thinning.
prereg.rationale: Two well-documented horizon effects line up in this setup: time-series momentum at daily-to-monthly horizons (Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen 2012; Menkhoff, Sarno, Schmeling & Schrimpf 2012 for FX) and short-horizon reversal of liquidity-driven moves (Lehmann 1990; Jegadeesh 1990; Grossman & Miller 1988 temporary price impact). A drop to the prior day's low while the daily trend is up is a one-day counter-move against the slower trend, the classic 'buy the pullback in a trend' configuration. The prior day's high/low is the most widely watched intraday reference on every daily chart; protective sell stops of existing longs and breakout-sell orders cluster just beyond it (Osler 2003, 2005: stop-loss orders cluster beyond salient price levels and execute as market orders). The first breach of the day converts that resting liquidity into market sells; when the same hour closes back above the level the triggered supply was absorbed without acceptance below, and inside a daily uptrend the absorbing side is the slower trend-following / dip-buying money whose demand persists for days. With the stop-loss supply exhausted the next day should drift with the daily trend. The trade is a daily-timeframe idea (daily trend, daily level), so its invalidation buffer is a quarter of a DAILY ATR beyond the wick: an hourly-scaled buffer sits inside one hour's noise, and the hold is one trading day (24 H1 bars).
prereg.novelty: S1-S13/N-series used H1-only context. S2 used previous-day/week levels with no trend condition, any breach, UTC-calendar days and a 0.25 x H1-ATR stop; S7/S8 conditioned on the 24-bar H1 return. MTF1 conditions on the DAILY trend from closed D1 bars (close vs 20-day SMA), trades only the trend-side level (PDL in uptrends, PDH in downtrends), only the first breach of that level in the trading day (stops still resting), builds FX/metal daily bars on the New York 17:00 close rather than UTC midnight, and scales the stop buffer to the daily ATR (0.25 x daily ATR is about 1.4 H1 ATRs, ~6x the 0.25 x H1-ATR pad), with no take-profit at the opposite pool (unlike N1). A daily-uptrend PDL sweep is usually AGAINST the 24h move, so it is neither S7 nor a plain S8 subset.
prereg.data_informed_note: Disclosed: the daily-ATR stop buffer was chosen knowing fact (a) (sweep fades have a small gross edge erased by costs because 0.25 x H1-ATR stops are ~0.8 ATR away and 77-80% are hit), and the designer had seen that S8 (against the 24h trend) printed less negative than S7 (with it). No result of this rule or any variant was computed; constants are defaults fixed before the first check.

prereg.family: fair-value-gap retest x time-series momentum (trend-aligned continuation)
prereg.desc: Step 1 (FVG1, unchanged): generate the registered FVG1 signals exactly as in P_FVG1.py (sha256 cd1f4a60...). Bullish FVG formed at bar k: low[k] > high[k-2]; middle bar k-1 bullish (close>open) and spanning the gap (low[k-1] <= high[k-2] and high[k-1] >= low[k]); gap height low[k]-high[k-2] >= 0.5*ATR14 at the close of bar k-2. Track for at most 120 bars from k+1; the FIRST bar i>k with low[i] <= low[k] is the only retest: if close[i] > low[k] -> LONG candidate at the open of bar i+1, otherwise the gap is mitigated and dropped. ext = min(low[k-2], low[k-1], low[i]). Bearish mirror (high[k] < low[k-2], bearish spanning middle bar, first retest high[i] >= high[k] with close[i] < high[k] -> SHORT candidate, ext = max(high[k-2], high[k-1], high[i])). Several same-side retests on one bar: the most recently formed gap defines ext; long and short retests on the same bar: no trade. Step 2 (trend filter, new): trend[i] = sign(ln close[i] - ln close[i-480]) computed on H1 bar positions (480 H1 bars = about 20 trading days for USDJPY/XAUUSD/XAGUSD and 20 calendar days for SOLUSDT). Keep the FVG1 signal at bar i only if side == trend[i]; drop it if trend[i] is 0 or undefined (i < 480 or non-finite closes). Trade: enter at the open of bar i+1, stop = ext - side*0.25*ATR14(at close of i), exit at the close of bar i+24 or at the stop; no take-profit; weight w = 1. Harness thinning (signals within 24 bars of a taken one ignored) applies as for FVG1.
prereg.rationale: A three-bar fair-value gap is the footprint of an aggressive parent order (meta-order) that consumed liquidity faster than it was replenished; a first retest that wicks into the gap and closes back outside it shows that the same participant (or the passive interest it left behind) is still defending price. Meta-order persistence is not homogeneous: order flow that is aligned with the slow, multi-week direction of the market is more likely to come from slow-moving capital (real-money rebalancing, macro/carry positioning, CTA and other trend-following flows, hedgers adjusting over days) whose execution is spread over many hours and days, so the unfilled remainder keeps working after the retest. Time-series momentum itself is attributed to under-reaction and to this gradual capital deployment (Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen 2012; Hurst, Ooi & Pedersen). Counter-trend displacements, by contrast, are more often liquidity events (stop runs, short-covering, news spikes against the prevailing flow) whose impact decays and reverts, so their retests should hold less often. Conditioning a short-horizon continuation entry on the sign of the slow trend therefore combines two weakly informative, largely independent signals (a three-bar intraday imbalance and a 20-day return) that point the same way, which should raise the per-trade edge of the continuation over the following 24 hours.
prereg.novelty: S1-S13, K1-K3 and N1-N8 fade or follow wicks through reference liquidity levels or use Kev; none uses imbalances or multi-week momentum. S7 (sweep with the 24h trend) and round-1 MTF1 combine a trend with a REVERSAL entry (a sweep fade) and both failed. R2B combines a slow trend (20-day TSMOM sign, not a 24h trend) with a CONTINUATION entry (first rejected retest of a displacement gap), i.e. both components point in the direction of the prevailing order flow. Round-1 FVG1 is the unfiltered event set; round-1 TSMOM1 trades Donchian breakouts with a 2N stop and 240-bar hold, whereas R2B uses the momentum sign only as a filter on 24-bar FVG trades.
prereg.notes: Round-2 lens, data-informed: chosen because round-1 FVG1 and TSMOM1 were each reported positive on 3 of 4 instruments (FVG1: USDJPY, SOL, XAU; TSMOM1: SOL, XAU, XAG). No profit/loss, R or win rate of this rule or any variant was computed by the designer; only 'eval_proposal.py check' (causality, counts, long share) was run. Parameters are not tuned: everything from FVG1 is copied verbatim and the lookback is the canonical one-month (20 trading day) TSMOM horizon expressed in H1 bars (480 = 20 x 24); no alternative lookback was examined. Bar positions are used instead of calendar time, so weekends and holidays are skipped for FX/metals (metals trade about 23 bars a day, so 480 bars is about 21 trading days). Expected risk: FVG1's tight stop is kept (cost/R about 0.08-0.11), so the filter must raise the per-trade gross edge substantially for P1/P3.

prereg.family: high-volatility sweep fade (S1 + elevated-volatility state filter)
prereg.desc: Events E = sweep_lib.events(df, name): every bar i that wicks through one of PDH/PDL (previous completed day high/low), PWH/PWL (previous completed week high/low), ASH/ASL (today's hours 0-6 range, usable from hour 7), SWH/SWL (latest 5-bar fractal swing, usable from pivot+3) or the round number above/below the bar's open, with open and close back on the near side of the level (upper level: high > X, open < X, close < X -> SHORT; lower level: low < X, open > X, close > X -> LONG); several levels swept in the same direction by one bar give one event, bars that swept both sides are dropped. side = E.side, ext = E.ext (the sweep bar's extreme: low for longs, high for shorts), atr = E.atr (ATR14 = 14-bar mean true range known before bar i, i.e. A[i-1]). FILTER (the only change from S1): A = sweep_lib.atr(df); v[i] = A[i-1] / median(A[i-2400 .. i-1]) where the median is a rolling 2400-bar median with min_periods 1200 (no value -> no trade); keep the event only if v[i] >= 1.5. Trade: enter at the open of bar i+1 in direction side; stop = ext - side*0.25*atr; no take-profit; exit at the close of the 24th bar after entry (H=24) or at the stop; weight w = 1. Same rule on all four instruments; overlapping signals are thinned by the harness (gap 24 bars).
prereg.rationale: (1) Liquidity-provision premium rises with volatility. Returns to short-term reversal / liquidity provision are strongly increasing in market volatility (Nagel 2012, RFS, 'Evaporating Liquidity'): when volatility is high, liquidity suppliers face higher inventory risk and funding constraints and withdraw, so a larger share of each price move is transient price pressure rather than information, and the expected compensation for taking the other side of that pressure rises. A sweep fade is a liquidity-provision trade: it buys the forced selling that ran the stops below a visible low (sells the forced buying above a high) after the bar has already closed back inside the level, i.e. after the pressure has started to be absorbed. If the small gross edge of S1 (+0.04..+0.10R, fact (a)) is a liquidity-provision premium, it should be concentrated in elevated-volatility states, when stop runs are larger relative to the depth available to absorb them. (2) Mechanical cost relief. Round-trip cost is a fixed price amount (USDJPY) or fixed fraction of price (others), equal to about 0.067/0.072/0.108/0.107 of a median H1 ATR on USDJPY/SOL/XAU/XAG, while the S1 stop distance scales with ATR (~0.8 ATR). When ATR is at least 1.5x its 100-day median, cost per R falls by a third or more, which is precisely the drag (0.10-0.16R) that erased S1's gross edge. (3) Consistency with the volatility-state evidence: S5 (sweep fades after compression) was the worst S-variant, and fact (b) says volatility state is persistent/predictable at the 24h horizon; together they suggest the fade edge is increasing in volatility state, so the opposite (elevated) state is the natural place to look. The 2400-bar median is a slow causal baseline that adapts to each instrument's secular volatility level, so the filter selects 'unusually volatile for this market' rather than 'volatile in absolute terms'.
prereg.novelty: Every earlier volatility condition used COMPRESSION: S5 faded sweeps during 12/120 std-ratio compression, N6 followed sweep wicks 1-6 bars after a compression release, VREG1 (batch) follows a close out of a compressed 12-bar box. None conditioned on an ELEVATED volatility state. EXH1 (batch) follows a single >= 3x ATR range-shock bar closing beyond a fresh level; R2A has no single-bar shock condition, uses a slow state measure (prior ATR14 vs its 2400-bar median) and FADES ordinary S1 sweeps. S12/S13 widened the stop to 1 ATR on all events; R2A keeps S1's stop and lowers cost/R only through the state selection. S2-S11 filter by level type, multiplicity, confirmation, wick shape, trend or structure, never by volatility regime.
prereg.notes: Round-2 lens. data_informed=True because the idea was shaped by fact (a) (S1's gross edge is smaller than costs), fact (b) (volatility state predicts the next-24h range), S5's result (compression fades were the worst S-variant) and the cost diagnostic (cost as a fraction of median ATR). Known risk: EXH1, which followed >= 3 ATR range-shock bars, was about 0 on USDJPY and the metals and +0.26 on SOL, so fading violent moves on SOL may lose. Constants (14, 2400, 1200, 1.5, H=24, pad=0.25, w=1) were fixed before the first 'check'; no profit/loss, R or win rate of this rule or any variant was computed or seen. Only 'eval_proposal.py check' (causality and counts) was run before registration.

prereg.family: time-series momentum, multi-horizon volatility-scaled composite (follow), signal-strength sizing
prereg.desc: Trading days are built from H1 bars exactly as in TSMOM1: the calendar date of the bar time, except that for USDJPY, XAUUSD and XAGUSD (closed on Saturday) bars stamped on a Sunday belong to the following Monday's day; SOLUSDT uses plain calendar dates. Daily close C[d] = last H1 close of trading day d; daily high/low = max/min of the day's H1 highs/lows; daily log return r[d] = ln(C[d]/C[d-1]); daily true range TR[d] = max(H-L, |H-C[d-1]|, |L-C[d-1]|). SIGNAL BAR i = the FIRST H1 bar of each trading day d; it uses only completed days up to d-1 (computed on daily bars, then shifted one trading day). sigma = sample std (ddof=1) of the 60 daily log returns r[d-60..d-1]. For L in {20, 60, 120}: s_L = ln(C[d-1]/C[d-1-L]) / (sigma * sqrt(L)). Composite S = arithmetic mean of s20, s60, s120 (NaN if any is NaN, i.e. fewer than 121 completed days). N = mean TR over the 20 completed days d-20..d-1. Skip the day if S is NaN or 0, or N is not > 0. side = sign(S) (+1 long, -1 short); weight w = min(|S|, 2.0); stop anchor ext = close[i] - side*2*N (pad = 0, so the stop is 2N from the signal close, Turtle 2N); atr = N. No take-profit. Enter at the open of bar i+1, exit at the close of the 120th bar after entry (H = 120, about one trading week) or at the stop. Signals within 120 bars of a taken signal are ignored (harness thinning), so the system holds at most one position, re-decided about every 5 (SOL, USDJPY) to 6 (metals, ~23 bars/day) trading days, always in the direction of the composite trend. Same rule and constants on all four instruments; the result is the w-weighted mean R.
prereg.rationale: Time-series momentum is one of the best-replicated effects in futures, FX and commodities (Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen 2012; Hurst, Ooi & Pedersen's century of evidence; Baltas & Kosowski 2013). Mechanisms: (1) slow diffusion of and initial under-reaction to fundamental information (policy divergence and carry for USDJPY, real rates / USD and industrial demand for gold and silver, capital flows into crypto), followed by delayed over-reaction as trend followers and momentum investors join; (2) pro-cyclical hedging and risk flows (dealer short-gamma hedging, stop-outs, margin calls, CTA vol-targeted rebalancing) that push price further in the trend direction; (3) the trend premium is a compensation/behavioural effect that is broad-based across horizons rather than tied to a single look-back, so averaging the 1-, 3- and 6-month vol-scaled returns diversifies horizon risk (Hurst-Ooi-Pedersen's equal-weight 1/3/12-month blend) and reduces whipsaw at any single channel boundary. Volatility-scaling (dividing by sigma*sqrt(L)) turns each horizon's return into a t-statistic-like trend strength that is comparable across instruments and regimes; Baltas & Kosowski show continuous, strength-weighted signals beat sign-only signals because weak, noisy trends (|S| near 0) carry little expected drift but full risk, so sizing by w = min(|S|, 2) puts capital where the trend evidence is strong and caps the weight where very large scores mostly reflect a just-completed spike. Daily re-decision with a weekly hold keeps the system always aligned with the current composite trend (unlike TSMOM1's event entries), gives 3-4x as many independent trades, and the 2N daily stop keeps round-trip cost at about 0.01R (USDJPY 1 pip vs ~150+ pips of risk), removing the cost failure mode of the H1 sweep fades (fact (a)).
prereg.novelty: All 24 REPORT.md methods react to intraday liquidity levels (PDH/PDL, PWH/PWL, Asian range, fractals, round numbers, clusters, equal highs/lows) with H1-ATR stops, 24-48 bar horizons and mostly FADE. Among the batch, TSMOM1 enters only on a fresh first H1 close beyond the 20-day Donchian channel (event-driven, sign-only, w=1, H=240); R2B uses a TSMOM direction only as a filter on FVG retests with H1 stops. R2C is the first method that (i) takes a position every trading-day decision point regardless of any price event (a continuous TSMOM rule), (ii) combines three look-back horizons into one volatility-scaled score, and (iii) uses the untried sizing modality w (signal-strength weight) instead of equal weight.
prereg.notes: data_informed=True: the lens (multi-horizon TSMOM with weekly hold and strength sizing) was proposed by the lead after seeing round-1 results, in particular that TSMOM1 was the strongest round-1 result (gold/silver P5 true, SOL and XAU positive) while its n at H=240 could not reach P3. The constants are canonical literature values (see module docstring) and were not chosen from any result; no P&L/R/win rate of this rule or any variant was computed; only 'eval_proposal.py check' (causality + counts) was run. Known risks disclosed in advance: (1) TSMOM1 signals were 61-68% long on all four instruments, so SOL/gold gains may be drift capture; the check output reports the long share, and results should also be read by side. (2) USDJPY 2016-20 was range-bound and TSMOM1 lost there (-0.25R); that era is the likely P2 failure. Bar times are broker server time (not necessarily UTC); the trading-day construction follows TSMOM1 for comparability. R is measured in units of 2N, so an equal-R trade is already inverse-volatility sized; w adds only the trend-strength tilt.

prereg.family: time-of-day USD order-flow seasonality (two legs per day, drift-neutral)
prereg.desc: Treat bar times as UTC (bar index = bar OPEN time). Convert each bar's open time to Asia/Tokyo (UTC+9, no DST) and to America/New_York (DST-aware, IANA tz). Define usd = +1 for USDJPY_H1 (price rises when USD strengthens) and usd = -1 for XAUUSD_H1, XAGUSD_H1 and SOLUSDT_H1 (USD/USDT-quoted: price falls when USD strengthens). Two fixed legs per day, the same rule on all four instruments. (1) TOKYO LEG: every bar whose open time is 08:00 Asia/Tokyo (= 23:00 UTC of the previous UTC date) on a Tokyo weekday (Monday-Friday of the Asia/Tokyo date, so Monday's leg is signalled by the Sunday 23:00 UTC bar) is a signal bar with side = +usd (LONG USD: USDJPY long; gold, silver, SOL short). Entry at the open of the next bar (09:00 JST); time exit at the close of the 8th bar after entry (H = 8, i.e. 17:00 JST when bars are contiguous). (2) NEW YORK LEG: every bar whose open time is 07:00 America/New_York (11:00 UTC under EDT, 12:00 UTC under EST) on a New York weekday (Monday-Friday of the New York date) is a signal bar with side = -usd (SHORT USD: USDJPY short; gold, silver, SOL long). Entry at the open of the next bar (08:00 ET); time exit at the close of the 8th bar after entry (16:00 ET). If the signal bar does not exist (holiday, data gap) there is no trade for that leg; holding is positional (8 bars), never conditioned on later bars. For both legs: ext = close of the signal bar i, atr = sweep_lib.atr(df) (ATR14 including bar i, known at its close), stop = ext - side*3.0*atr (a catastrophe stop only, ~3 H1 ATR from entry), no take-profit, weight w = 1. No price, volume, volatility or trend condition of any kind: the trade is unconditional on the clock. Legs of one day are >= 10 bars apart, so thinning with gap H = 8 keeps both.
prereg.rationale: Ranaldo (2009, Journal of Banking & Finance, 'Segmentation and time-of-day patterns in foreign exchange markets') and Breedon & Ranaldo (2013, Journal of Money, Credit and Banking, 'Intraday patterns in FX returns and order flow') document that currencies systematically depreciate during their own domestic trading hours and appreciate during foreign hours. Breedon & Ranaldo tie the pattern to order flow: domestic investors and corporates are net buyers of foreign currency during their own business hours (importers, outward portfolio investment, hedging by domestic institutions executed through domestic dealers), which pushes the home currency down while home dealers are the main liquidity takers, and the inventory is unwound when the foreign centre opens. The effect is a liquidity/inventory premium paid by predictable, clock-driven flow, not information, so it should be unconditional on price and should not need a level or a trigger. Two legs per day follow directly: (1) Tokyo business hours (09:00-17:00 JST): JPY is the domestic currency, so JPY should weaken, i.e. USDJPY rises (long USD); (2) New York business hours (08:00-16:00 ET): USD is the domestic currency, so USD should weaken, i.e. USDJPY falls, gold, silver and SOL (USD-quoted) rise. USDJPY therefore has double support on both legs (JPY-domestic in Tokyo, USD-domestic in New York). For XAU, XAG and SOL the pattern is an out-of-sample prediction of a USD-wide domestic-flow effect: if US-hours USD selling is a broad dollar flow, dollar-quoted assets should rise in US hours and give it back (USD stronger) in Asian hours. Pairing a long-USD leg with a short-USD leg every day makes net exposure about zero, so the strong secular drifts of SOL, gold and USDJPY in 2021-25 cannot by themselves produce a positive mean. Entry and exit times are the canonical local business-day boundaries (09:00-17:00 JST; 08:00-16:00 ET, the start of the NY dealing day to the US cash close), not tuned; the 3-ATR stop exists only to cap tail risk on event days so that R is essentially the 8-hour return scaled by 3 H1 ATR, which keeps cost per R small (USDJPY 1 pip is ~0.02-0.03R).
prereg.novelty: This is the first UNCONDITIONAL time-of-day test in the programme. S1-S13, K1-K4 and N1-N8 trade sweeps of price levels (previous day/week, Asian range, fractal swings, round numbers) with stops beyond the wick. In this batch SESS1 trades a conditional New York opening-range breakout (direction set by price), CAL1 trades a conditional month-end/London-fix price-pressure reversal, and N3 faded a conditional sweep of the Asian range at the London open (07-08h); none of them holds a fixed-direction position over a fixed clock window every day. R2D's direction is set only by the clock and the instrument's USD orientation (never by price), it has two opposite-sign legs per day (drift-neutral by construction), its stop is a 3-ATR catastrophe stop rather than a level, and it is not an inversion of any failed method.
prereg.notes: Round-2 lens. data_informed=True because the lens was chosen after round-1 results (sweep fades: gross edge smaller than costs with ~0.8 ATR stops; conditional session/fix methods SESS1/CAL1/N3 already tested), which motivated a wide-stop, cost-light, unconditional clock trade from the FX-seasonality literature. The rule, legs, directions, hours, H, pad and w come from that literature and the session clock; no profit/loss, R, return or win rate of this rule or any variant was computed or seen. Only 'eval_proposal.py check' (causality and counts) was run before registration. Disclosure: after the rule was written, a grep for 'N3' (to describe N3 correctly in 'novelty') printed N3's stored round-1 result line from OVERNIGHT_RUNS.txt (a different, failed sweep method); nothing in R2D was changed because of it. Known risks: (i) at an 8-hour hold 1 pip is roughly 0.03-0.04 of the 8-hour return std on USDJPY, so costs subtract ~2.5-3.5 t-units over ~7800 legs, and a real but small effect may still miss P1/P3 there; (ii) for metals there is a conflicting folk pattern (Asian-hours physical gold buying would make gold rise, not fall, in Tokyo hours); (iii) SOL/USDT is a 24/7 crypto market whose USD-flow link is weaker than for FX; (iv) the published FX evidence is mostly pre-2010, so the effect may have been arbitraged away. Expected non-overlapping counts ~7800 / 2800 / 4000 / 4000.
